name: Vatsyayana Pakshilasvamin
dates_notes: Dated by his pre-Diṅnāga doctrinal stratum and his being the named target of Diṅnāga's Pramāṇa-Samuccaya criticism; Vidyabhusana 1920 and Matilal 1977 converge on the late fourth or early fifth century CE. The Naiyāyika Vātsyāyana is to be sharply distinguished from the Vātsyāyana of the Kāma-Sūtra.
core_thesis: Vātsyāyana’s *Nyāya-Bhāṣya* is the earliest surviving commentary on the *Nyāya-Sūtra* and gives its compressed categories a systematic interpretation. It develops the four *pramāṇas* by distinguishing the instrument, object, and result of cognition, and elaborates Nyāya accounts of perception and inference. The commentary also argues for an enduring self against Buddhist no-self positions, using the continuity required for memory, cognition, action, and karmic fruition. Its treatment of absence contributes to later debates over *anupalabdhi* and the cognition of nonexistence. Vātsyāyana engages early Buddhist idealist arguments in defending the reality of external objects and the independence of testimony as a means of knowledge. The *Bhāṣya* became the primary base text for the Old Nyāya commentarial tradition.

engaged_works.title: Nyaya-Sutra-Bhashya
engaged_works.composition_dates_notes: Composition fixed by being the named target of Diṅnāga's Pramāṇa-Samuccaya (c. 480 CE).
engaged_works.ascription_notes: Securely authored prose commentary on the Nyāya-Sūtra; the foundational text of the Old-Nyāya commentarial stack.
engaged_works.summary: The earliest surviving prose commentary on the *Nyāya-Sūtra*, structured as *sūtra*-by-*sūtra* exposition through all five *adhyāyas*. The *bhāṣya*'s historical importance is twofold. First, it transforms the *Sūtra*'s lapidary statements into a workable system: definitions are unpacked, technical distinctions are introduced, and the relations among the sixteen *padārthas* ([NS 1.1.1](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.1.1)) are made explicit. The treatment of *pratyakṣa* under [NS 1.1.4](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.1.4) — including the *savikalpaka*–*nirvikalpaka* distinction and the analysis of perceptual cognition as *indriyārtha-saṃnikarṣa-janya* — is the locus classicus for the Naiyāyika theory of perception that all later commentators presuppose. Second, the *bhāṣya* opens the long polemic against Buddhist epistemology that defines the school's external posture for the next millennium: the defense of the *ātman* against *nairātmya-vāda* ([NS 1.1.10](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/1.1.10) and 3.1.1 onward), the defense of extra-mental objects against the proto-Yogācāra denial (on [NS 4.2.26–37](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/4.2.26-37)), the defense of the *prāmāṇya* of perception against radical skepticism (on [NS 2.1.8–20](cite://sureshvara/naishkarmya-siddhi/2.1.8-20)). The *bhāṣya* attracts Diṅnāga's *Pramāṇa-Samuccaya* (chapter 1, *pratyakṣa*; chapter 5, *apoha*) as its principal opponent; Uddyotakara's *Nyāya-Vārttika* in turn replies to Diṅnāga while extending the *bhāṣya*. The Vāchaspati Miśra → Udayana commentarial line is built on the *bhāṣya* as base.
